item.title: Asymmetry between the major parties fries the circuits of the mainstream press - PressThink
item.description: Rosen analyzes the challenges faced by mainstream political journalism during the 2016 US presidential election campaign, particularly in covering Donald Trump. Rosen argues that the traditional journalistic framework, based on the assumption of symmetry between the two major parties, is inadequate for understanding Trump's unconventional candidacy and the resulting asymmetric polarization. He proposes three key propositions: 1) Political journalism relies on a shared mental picture of politics that assumes similar actors with 'warring philosophies'; 2) This symmetry is disrupted by the Republican Party's extreme stance and Trump's disregard for facts and norms; and 3) The media's failure to adapt to this asymmetry resembles 'technical debt', leading to a distorted representation of reality.

item.title: So I will try to explain why the Trump candidacy has been so confounding to our political press. - PressThink
item.description: Rosen analyzes the changing dynamics of political journalism in the context of the 2016 US presidential election, particularly the impact of Donald Trump's campaign. Rosen argues that the traditional 'laws of political gravity' governing campaign coverage, based on shared assumptions within the political class and media, have broken down. This breakdown is attributed to Trump's disregard for established norms and the media's struggle to adapt, leading to homogeneity in coverage and a lack of clear purpose. Rosen contrasts this with the approach of Jorge Ramos, who demonstrates a clear sense of purpose and audience representation, illustrating an alternative model for political journalism.

item.title: Verstehen, was den Journalismus derzeit verändert
item.description: Journalism is undergoing significant changes, and many struggle to understand them, often getting caught between condemning the new digital landscape or clinging to the old ways. The core issue lies in the fact that journalists are products of the changing society they are trying to understand, making it hard for them to objectively assess their own role. To better comprehend these shifts, media houses and journalists must observe society, technology, science, economics, and politics, recognizing patterns and connections rather than judging individual phenomena. Breaking down silos and fostering collaboration among various professionals is crucial to understanding and shaping the future of journalism and remaining relevant in a constantly evolving world.

item.title: Comment être au courant de ce qui change le journalisme ?
item.description: To stay informed about the evolving landscape of journalism, one should utilize various resources. Newsletters like La Matinale du Monde and Le 5 à 7 de l’AFP provide key information. Specialized websites such as Journalisme.com and Arrêt sur images offer in-depth analysis. Books like “Le Journalisme sans journalistes” and “La Fabrication de l’information” offer deeper insights. Blogs and Twitter accounts, including those of Daniel Schneidermann and Slate.fr, provide real-time updates and commentary.

item.title: The Studio 2.0 Program at NYU (directed by Jay Rosen and Clay Shirky) once again presents Open Studio Night!
item.description: Studio 2.0 at NYU, co-directed by Jay Rosen and Clay Shirky, is hosting its second Open Studio Night. The event allows the program's twelve students to showcase their projects focused on the future of news, providing opportunities for interaction, feedback, and discussion. Attendees can learn about emerging trends in journalism. The event will be held on Wednesday, November 19, 2014, at the Studio 2.0 Room in New York, NY, and requires an RSVP. Studio 2.0 emphasizes experimentation and creation, encouraging students to build prototypes and design new services in response to changes in journalism. The program prioritizes invention and creation alongside critical thinking, with a focus on practical application.

item.title: Rosen's Trust Puzzler: What Explains Falling Confidence in the Press? - PressThink
item.description: Rosen explores the declining public trust in news media despite improvements in journalistic professionalism. Rosen presents several competing explanations, including the general decline in trust across institutions, the negative influence of bad actors in media, accusations of liberal bias, strategic manipulation of journalists ('working the refs'), and a potential misalignment between journalistic professionalization and public needs. Rosen concludes that none of these explanations fully capture the complexity of the issue and invites further discussion.

item.title: Real reporting is about revealing truth; not granting 'equal weight' to bogus arguments
item.description: Mike Masnick uses Jay Rosen’s critique of he-said/she-said reporting to argue that journalism should report what is true rather than give equal weight to weak claims. The article centers on New York Times coverage of plagiarism allegations involving Rick Perlstein and Craig Shirley, and cites Margaret Sullivan’s public-editor response.

item.title: When quoting both sides and leaving it there is the riskier call
item.description: Rosen critiques the 'he said, she said' approach in journalism, arguing that in situations where facts are verifiable, presenting both sides equally can be reckless and even misleading. Rosen uses examples from the New York Times' coverage of plagiarism accusations against a book and the BBC's handling of climate change reporting to illustrate how clinging to false equivalence can confer legitimacy on false claims and distort the truth. Rosen contends that the old standard of 'no position' is increasingly risky and that newsrooms need to evolve beyond this approach.
